vignette:
She is 80 now, a South Asian woman who still introduces herself first as a dentist, even though she works only a few mornings a week and no longer keeps the punishing schedule she once did. She speaks with the careful precision of someone used to calming frightened patients. In the first sessions, she tells her story the way she learned to deliver difficult news in the clinic-plainly, without embellishment. But the shape of it becomes clearer over time: a life divided into before and after one morning of terrorism.

Years ago, she is in her dental office, already in her white coat, reviewing charts before the first patient. The practice sits on a busy commercial street, the kind of place where people buy tea, pick up prescriptions, argue over parking spaces. She remembers the ordinary details with painful clarity: the smell of clove oil, the hum of the sterilizer, the receptionist laughing at something on the phone. Then comes a sound she first mistakes for construction-an enormous crack, followed by another, and then screaming. The front windows shudder. A man runs past outside, his face bloodied, and someone in the waiting room drops to the floor. She does not understand immediately that it is an attack. She only knows the world has become noise, dust, and terror.

She corrals her staff and the two waiting patients into the back sterilization room and locks the door. She can hear more blasts, shouts, sirens, then a silence that feels even worse. One of her patients, a young mother, is crying and trying to call her children. The dentist in her takes over. She speaks steadily, counts breaths, wets gauze for a cut on the receptionist's forehead, and keeps everyone low to the ground. Inside, though, she is certain they may die behind that flimsy door. Even now, when she describes it, she presses her palms together so hard her knuckles pale.

In the days afterward, she returns too quickly to work. She tells herself this is strength, discipline, survival. She has lived through political unrest before, the sort of instability many in her generation learned to absorb without complaint. But this is different. The street outside her clinic has changed in her mind. Every unattended bag, every motorcycle backfiring, every raised voice sends a bolt through her chest. She starts scanning windows and exits everywhere she goes. She positions patients' chairs so she can see the door. If someone arrives late and agitated, she feels sweat gather under her collar.

At night, the attack replays not always as a full nightmare, but in fragments: shattered glass in her hair, the mother's shaking hands, the strange pause between explosion and screaming. She wakes already braced, heart pounding, listening for sounds that are not there. She becomes reluctant to sleep deeply because sleep means losing watchfulness. On those nights she goes to the kitchen, makes tea, and sits in the dark rather than risk dreaming.

Her family notices changes she does not name. Long divorced and proud of her independence, she has managed her life for decades without leaning much on anyone. After the attack, she grows more rigid, then more withdrawn. Her adult children call and she says she is fine, always fine. She no longer enjoys crowded weddings, religious gatherings, or the noisy family dinners she once hosted with elaborate care. If relatives begin discussing current events or another bombing somewhere in the world, she leaves the room or snaps at them with surprising sharpness. Later she feels ashamed and retreats further.

Work, once the steadiest part of her identity, becomes both refuge and burden. In the operatory she can still be competent, exacting, useful. Yet she startles when instruments clatter onto a tray. The suction's high whine sometimes blends in her mind with sirens. A patient's sudden movement can flood her with a moment of unreality in which the walls of the clinic seem thin and unsafe. She dislikes admitting fear, so she tells colleagues she is simply tired, simply aging. But she begins canceling full clinic days, then reducing her hours. She says she wants balance. Privately, she fears she can no longer trust her own nerves.

She avoids the block where the attack happened unless she must go there. Even after the building is repaired, she cannot look at the replaced windows without seeing them burst inward. Certain smells-burned wiring, dust after roadwork-transport her instantly. On those days she becomes irritable and distracted, misplacing charts, rereading the same page, forgetting why she walked into a room. She worries this means her mind is failing. Yet when the subject changes, her memory is sharp, almost too sharp, especially for that morning.

In the present, she sits upright in the consulting room, elegantly dressed, her handbag placed squarely by her feet as if ready for quick departure. She still notices every hallway sound. She still maps exits without meaning to. She says she has spent a lifetime calming pain in other people while learning to clench around her own. What troubles her most is not only fear, but the narrowing of her world. She has survived, built a career, raised children, endured divorce, migration, and aging. Still, a part of her remains in that locked back room, listening for the next blast, waiting for permission to believe that ordinary life is safe again.
